title: Ledger and Regiment
premise: In 1804, Hazel Hartwell, a mapmaker's apprentice in the port city of Wexbridge, is completing the coastal atlas her master died surveying when war orders arrive and the harbor begins emptying. A sealed letter found among his papers names her family as holders of a deed the Admiralty wants buried — and entangles her with Elias Vane, the master's estranged son, now an officer on the enemy side of the channel. Pursued by a naval clerk determined to seize the atlas and the deed alike, Hazel must choose between the inheritance that would legitimize her nameless birth and the promise she made to deliver the finished atlas to Elias before his ship sails on the morning tide. She keeps the promise at cost of the deed, burns what cannot be carried, and claims her identity not by paper but by the map itself, published under her own hand.
about_author: Wendell Pemberton is a former hydrographic surveyor who spent a decade charting coastlines before turning to fiction, drawn to the quiet dramas hidden inside official records. He writes from a cluttered study overlooking a working harbor, where he collects antique instruments and unfinished maps.

chapters.title: The Weight of Coastlines
chapters.summary: Hazel, POV, finishes inking the final plate of Master Aldous Hartwell's coastal atlas two years after his death, measuring her life in what fits in a satchel. The emotional beat is quiet grief braided with pride of craft, as she signs nothing, being only the apprentice.

chapters.title: Orders for the Harbor
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV: press notices appear and the Admiralty requisitions charts; her patron Mr. Quill warns the atlas may be seized as state property. She hides the master plates behind a false wall. The beat is the first tremor of a world reordering itself around her.

chapters.title: A Letter Under Seal
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV: sorting the master's effects, she finds a sealed letter naming 'Hartwell' among signatories of an old deed to the tidal flats — land the Navy now needs. The beat is dread: inheritance arriving as accusation rather than gift.

chapters.title: The Clerk with Clean Hands
chapters.summary: POV shifts to Naval Clerk Ambrose Fitch, who arrives politely demanding all Hartwell papers. Hazel lies smoothly about their existence. The beat is a duel of courtesies, establishing Fitch as patient, legal, and utterly relentless.

chapters.title: What the Master Promised
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV: the letter reveals Aldous promised his estranged son Elias a finished copy of the atlas — a promise made in peacetime, before Elias took a commission across the channel. The beat is conflicted loyalty: keeping it means aiding a declared enemy.

chapters.title: Deed and Name
chapters.summary: Hazel visits the registry and learns the deed could legitimize her — Aldous never formally adopted her, and the land would make 'Hartwell' legally hers. The beat is hunger for belonging, sharpened by how easily Fitch could erase her claim.

chapters.title: Fitch Returns
chapters.summary: Fitch's POV: he suspects the plates exist and offers Hazel protection in exchange for them, hinting the family name is already listed for investigation. The beat is seduction of safety, and Hazel's refusal costs her his civility.

chapters.title: The False Wall
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV: she moves the atlas plates by night through the ropewalk to her friend Tamsin's sail loft, carrying the world in pieces on her back. The beat is exhilaration turning to fear when she realizes she was followed.

chapters.title: Elias, From a Distance
chapters.summary: Elias Vane's POV aboard the frigate Cerberus at anchor off Wexbridge roads: he has come under cover of a survey errand to see whether his father's work survived him. The beat is longing for a father he quarreled with, and curiosity about the apprentice whose letters he once read aloud.

chapters.title: A Meeting on the Mudflats
chapters.summary: Hazel and Elias meet secretly on the tidal flats where Aldous died surveying. They exchange truths: the deed, the promise, the danger. The beat is recognition between two people both disinherited by the same man's silences.

chapters.title: Listed
chapters.summary: Fitch's POV: he files the Hartwell name for seizure and intercepts a note meant for Elias, confirming collusion. The beat is cold satisfaction — Fitch believes he is serving order, not malice, which makes him worse.

chapters.title: Tamsin's Bargain
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV: Tamsin agrees to hide the plates inside a consignment of sails bound for a neutral trader, but demands Hazel decide within three days what she truly wants — the deed or the promise. The beat is forced clarity.

chapters.title: The Registry Burns Late
chapters.summary: Hazel returns to copy the deed before Fitch can void it and finds the registry office ransacked, the record torn out. Someone got there first. The beat is vertigo: her inheritance exists now only in memory and rumor.

chapters.title: Quill's Confession
chapters.summary: Old Quill admits he tipped off Fitch years ago about the deed, believing cooperation would protect the workshop, and begs Hazel's forgiveness. The beat is betrayal softened into tragedy — everyone bargained with the same machine.

chapters.title: What Can Be Carried
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV: she reduces the atlas to one master plate and the fair-copy atlas itself, burning drafts and letters that could hang her. The beat is ritual loss — identity pared down to essentials, echoing the theme of measure.

chapters.title: Fitch Closes In
chapters.summary: Fitch raids the sail loft with a warrant; Tamsin covers for Hazel at real personal risk, and the plates are nearly discovered. The beat is terror and gratitude, cementing chosen family against blood and crown alike.

chapters.title: The Night Tide
chapters.summary: Hazel rows out to the Cerberus at night to deliver the atlas to Elias, evading the harbor watch. Elias gives her the recovered deed page he tore from the registry — his own act of inheritance refused. The beat is the promise kept, and love acknowledged without time to name it.

chapters.title: Morning Tide
chapters.summary: Dual POV: as the Cerberus weighs anchor, Fitch boards Hazel's workshop with soldiers and finds walls stripped bare. Elias watches Wexbridge shrink from the quarterdeck, the atlas lashed to his chest. The beat is simultaneous departure and survival.

chapters.title: The Examination
chapters.summary: Fitch interrogates Hazel, laying out evidence thread by thread; she answers only with the truth that damns no one but herself — that she is no one's daughter, only a mapmaker. The beat is defiant self-invention under pressure.

chapters.title: The Atlas Speaks
chapters.summary: Fitch opens the seized fair-copy atlas and finds Aldous's dedication naming 'my apprentice, Hazel Hartwell, in her own hand' — written years before, making her authorship and the deed's intent undeniable. The beat is the dead master intervening; Fitch's case collapses into embarrassment.

chapters.title: Published Under Her Own Hand
chapters.summary: Months later, the atlas is printed with Hazel's name on the title page, the deed quietly settled as a pension and a small freehold. Tamsin, Quill, and the harbor community gather. The beat is belonging earned rather than inherited.

chapters.title: Soundings
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV, closing: she takes new apprentices and begins surveying the unmapped estuary, mailing a single chart to a neutral port addressed to E.V. The beat is open-ended hope — identity as ongoing work, like a coastline, never quite finished.
